text: Two additional important factors led to an over-estimate of the soil strength below the 17th Street Canal. First, the data shown in Figure 7.2 represent the values from borings drilled along the centerline of the levee over a distance of 8,000 feet — about 11⁄2 miles. Lumping together data over distances is not uncommon. text: The following sections describe key lessons learned based on our EPA OIG review of EPA’s response following the attack and collapse of the World Trade Center towers in New York, and the applicability of these lessons learned in responding to environmental concerns after Hurricane Katrina. In general, many of the concerns raised in EPA’s response to the collapse of the World Trade Center towers did not become an issue in responding to Katrina. This can likely be attributed to three factors: (1) some issues were not applicable to Katrina due to the uniqueness of the World Trade Center disaster; (2) for some issues that were applicable, EPA applied the lessons learned from the World Trade Center experience; and (3) unlike the World Trade disaster, EPA and States had experience in responding to prior hurricane disasters that helped prepare them to respond to Katrina. Each section below describes a key World Trade Center lessons learned, and how these concerns were handled, if applicable, with respect to the three major areas of the Katrina response we evaluated: drinking water, wastewater, and hazardous waste and debris management.

Second, although SBA’s new disaster loan processing system provides opportunities to streamline the loan origination process, it has experienced numerous outages and slow response times in accessing information. However, we have not yet determined the duration and impact of these outages on processing. SBA officials have attributed many of these problems to a combination of hardware and telecommunications capacity limitations as well as the level of service SBA has received from its contractors. text: The magnitude and severity of Hurricane Katrina and other recent catastrophes also impacted the insurance industry’s willingness and ability to provide insurance protection for catastrophic disasters. A crucial aspect of being able to successfully provide such coverage is the ability to obtain what the industry refers to as credible “vulnerability assessments” or risk assessments. To be useful, a risk assessment must be able to estimate both the likely “frequency” and “severity” of catastrophic events— two key characteristics that insurance companies need to assess the probability and financial significance of a loss. In addition, based on credible information, insurers must be able to estimate both their “probable maximum loss (PML),” an estimate of the maximum dollar value that can be lost under realistic conditions, and their “maximum foreseeable loss (MFL),” an estimate of the maximum dollar loss under a worst-case scenario. Risk assessments can be used to provide a basis for making loss projections for catastrophes such as hurricanes or earthquakes, although the projections may not be accurate. Insurance companies use these estimates to determine the amount of coverage and the price at which to offer coverage within a geographic area. Potential losses are acceptable if the probability that they may occur is understood and companies can set prices that fully reflect the consequences of a specific risk. When projections fail to anticipate an event, such as an earthquake, or underestimate the severity of an event, such as Hurricane Katrina, insurance companies may become insolvent, as happened in the aftermath of Hurricane Andrew, or may choose to reduce the amount of coverage offered in a given area, as happened for wind losses in Florida and for earthquakes in California.

text: Because catastrophic disasters are likely to occur in the future, and because forecasting their probability and severity is an inexact science, state insurance regulators have recommended that the federal government provide a final layer of insurance protection in the event of a “megacatastrophe.” The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) is considering a broad national plan that would create a mechanism to handle disasters, especially those larger than Hurricane Katrina. The plan proposes a public-private partnership that would reward hazard mitigation and spread catastrophic risk broadly among individual insureds, insurers, reinsurers, state reinsurance funds, and the federal government, according to NAIC. The federal government could provide a top layer of protection by acting as a reinsurer of last resort or, alternatively, by providing financial capacity to a multi-state risk pooling mechanism that could borrow from the federal government should catastrophic losses exceed the pool’s accumulated funds. This plan is similar in scope to the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA), which Congress enacted to create a program of shared public and private compensation for insured losses attributable to acts of terrorism. Under the NAIC plan, however, taxpayers would presumably not have to pay for losses. Furthermore, the NAIC plan asserts that if state and federal governments insured the top layers of catastrophe risk, private insurers would continue to insure the initial layer of risk that they might otherwise not insure.

text: What would another Hurricane Katrina bring in 2020? Is government at all levels ready for such an event? Or is the worst yet to come? (Kettl 2006). In the following sections, we argue that successful emergency preparedness, response, and recovery in the future are largely functions of the degree to which government leaders possess strategic management capacity. Such management is an ongoing process integrating planning that is issue focused, externally oriented, and opportunity seeking (Koteen 1997). We do not sound the alarm that is so common among post-9/11 and Katrina commentators, but rather offer a strategic framework to enhance our understanding of the importance of management and leadership before and during a Katrina-like event occurring in the year 2020. We cannot point to the characteristics of what an “ideal” response and recovery for any given situation or locale might look like in this short essay—if indeed such characteristics exist and could be identified—but we do offer perspectives on the critical managerial components of an emergency management strategy. Our observations are grounded in the notion that a “disaster occurs when the demands of the system are greater than the capabilities of the community to meet them” (Simpson 2008). Put another way, the impact of a disaster “agent” (such as a hurricane) alone does not determine whether an actual disaster occurred; it is also a question of whether the community has the requisite strategic capacity to effectively mitigate, address, and cope with the incident.

text: Because much of the blame for the overall ineffective response to Katrina is placed on the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), as the nation’s coordinating arm for natural disasters and catastrophes, we use FEMA as a lens through which strategic capacity can be assessed and developed. Nonetheless, because basic federal law and practice have never abandoned the principle that initial responsibility rests with first responders and local management, we also demonstrate the importance of the relationship between all levels of government, nongovernmental organizations, and the general public, and how planning and support at the federal level should fan out through the intergovernmental system. We can never be 100 percent sure whether any city, region, state, or nation is prepared for any given unique catastrophic event, but certain managerial principles can be established that will enable a government scarred by Katrina to do its best and to more effectively mitigate and plan, and carry out its response and recovery obligations in the future. We conclude by arguing that, five years after Katrina, progress is being made, but the gains need to be consistently supported and maintained, with substantially more to be accomplished. But first, we examine the state of emergency management in the United States in the years immediately preceding Hurricane Katrina.

In August 2005, the focus of reform efforts within the U.S. government was to support the “war on terror.” Federal efforts, strategic and operational plans, reorganizations, and budgets established after the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, reflected this focus. Prior to 9/11, under the George W. text: At the time of Hurricane Katrina, on August 29, 2005, emergency management and program content and fiscal support varied wildly by region and locality; state and local programs had barely had a chance to reorganize in support of the new war on terror expectations; and some of the people who filled emergency management–related positions had rather eclectic educational and professional backgrounds. Many brought with them ideas, standards, and communication and organizational skills influenced by their primary discipline or field. The content of local emergency plans reflected this diversity, ranging from those composed of simply an “evacuation plan” (a map and a description of major area routes) to a more mature, fully developed plan, complete with an identification and analysis of likely risks, personnel qualifications, memoranda of understanding of support between organizations, an evacuation plan based on likely hazards and computer modeling, and requirements for training, drills, and periodic exercises (Edwards and Goodrich 2007; Grant 1996).

text: At the time of Hurricane Katrina, the NRP was in place yet remained largely untested. It had been used for smaller emergencies prior to Katrina, but the hurricane marked the first time the NRP was used for a catastrophic event. Complicating matters further, FEMA headquarters and its 10 regions differed in their philosophies and cultures. Headquarters was responsible for setting policy, but each region was responsible for interpreting and implementing that policy. With political appointees heading up each FEMA region as well as headquarters, and FEMA overall weakened by its absorption into the Department of Homeland Security, regional administrators felt free to act independently, and to rely on their own judgment and that of the states and locals within their region. Conflict among regions and even between managers within a FEMA region and at headquarters occurred frequently (Olasky 2006; Sylves 2006).

text: It is hardly a surprise, then, that preparation for and the response to Hurricane Katrina resulted in failure. Shortly after the storm struck, Sandra Schneider asserts, “some of the major problems encountered during the response to Katrina stemmed from breakdowns in the administrative elements of the governmental emergency management system. Effective bureaucratic agencies are characterized by well-established procedures, effective leadership, and clear objectives. An early assessment suggests that problems associated with all three of these bureaucratic characteristics weakened governmental efforts to respond quickly and effectively” (2005, 515). State and local governments in Louisiana and Mississippi were simply overwhelmed following Hurricane Katrina. Failures and subsequent recommendations by the federal government are documented in reports issued by the U.S. House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate, and the White House, the last of which focused on the federal administrative response and offered a total of 125 recommendations in a multitude of areas, including review and revision of the NRP; increased involvement of the private sector and other nongovernmental organizations; the education and empowerment of citizens; and further integration and coordination of federal, state, and local efforts (U.S. House 2006; U.S. Senate 2006; White House 2006). However, little attention was given to strategic thinking and acting, and how incorporating strategic issues management into the bureaucratic process as well as intergovernmental coordination and collaboration might improve the management of future catastrophes.

text: The use of strategic issues management, which addresses the primary strategic concerns of an organization or organizational system, is important in emergency management because of the occurrence of unexpected and surprise events. Koteen (1997) argues that the criteria for identifying strategic issues include assessing (1) the current or potential impact on organizational performance, (2) the perceived urgency in significant consequences, and (3) the impact or interdependency with other issues. For more than three decades, emergency management has been described in terms of a comprehensive, systems-based approach to activities comprising four management phases: mitigation, planning and preparedness, response, and recovery. However, most of the academic and popular literature has focused on one phase—emergency response— even as Hurricane Katrina exposed weaknesses in mitigation and recovery. Effective strategic management of disasters necessarily must focus on all issues and phases.

text: Historically, major hurricanes have left in their wake fresh congressional enactments that enlarged the federal role in disaster response, and Katrina was no different. One of the first major casualties of the emergency management infrastructure overhaul was the National Response Plan. It was deemed difficult to understand and implement; at more than 400 pages, overly complicated and bureaucratic; and generally confusing (Birkland and Waterman 2008). Its development had effectively excluded the participation of nonfederal stakeholders, such as states and localities, and suffered from limited comment periods for all parties, including federal partners and the public.

text: In response to the post-Katrina legislation and perceived problems with the implementation of the NRP, the Department of Homeland Security substantially revised the plan, with more involvement from stakeholders, and reissued it in 2008 as the National Response Framework. In its final form, the National Response Framework is part of an overall national strategy for homeland security, attempting to build adaptability and flexibility into response efforts by setting up a general framework rather than a specific prescription. Its intent is to provide the doctrine and guiding principles for a unified response at all levels of government for all types of hazards, but to give users some latitude as to how they choose to respond.

text: FEMA is also attempting to effectively address the strategic issue of recovery from disasters. The National Disaster Recovery Framework (in draft form at the time of this writing) is intended to move beyond the scope of the National Response Framework. The draft National Disaster Recovery Framework offers a spectrum of recovery actions that begins, in the ideal situation, before a disaster strikes. It states that postdisaster recovery activities should begin, or should be acknowledged as beginning, in the early stages of response, and that actions to support recovery activities should be built into governmental operations at all levels. Like the National Response Framework’s philosophy of response, the draft National Disaster Recovery Framework recognizes the role of the federal government as a partner, coordinator, and facilitator, and notes that tribal, state, and local governments have primary responsibility for the recovery of their communities and play the lead role in planning and authority for managing all aspects of community recovery.

This desire for a stepby-step guide reflects (1) a failure of attention by local government planners to properly and thoroughly elucidate those involved, why, and how; (2) a gap in the extent to which learning occurs across and within communities that experience disasters; and (3) a need for street-level actors to know who in real time fulfills specific leadership and complementary roles. The frameworks guiding FEMA assume that federal, state, and local entities communicate and coordinate, and that localities establish and support over time the relationships, connectedness, and coordination essential for successful response and recovery. text: Disasters, by their very nature, typically exceed a single jurisdiction’s (or entity’s) ability or resources, and they almost never neatly contain themselves within a single city, county, or even state’s boundaries. Drabek and McEntire note that “disasters, by their very disruptive and dynamic nature, create such significant demands on the affected community that well-executed, multiorganizational responses become not only necessary, but essential... In addition, disasters often require the assistance of outsiders and multiple levels of government, thereby leading to multijurisdictional response operations” (2002, 206). Thus, the emergency management networks that characterize the field necessarily involve literally dozens of potential partners and sometimes thousands of volunteers. Petak explained long ago that, for emergency management, “understanding... the intergovernmental complexities may be of greater importance to the success of activities than scientific knowledge, technical remedies, or their associated economic cost and benefits” (1985, 4–5).

text: The National Response Framework provides a clear endorsement of the idea of locally led coordination in emergency management (DHS 2008). It defines the duties of local emergency managers as having the day-to-day authority and responsibility in their jurisdictions for overseeing emergency management programs and activities. The document states that the local emergency manager “coordinates all components of the local emergency management program,” and that includes coordinating the planning process; working collaboratively with other local agencies, which may include both nonprofit and for-profit organizations; and involving other organizations in planning, training, and exercises. Indeed, creating engaged partnerships is the first principle listed in the document. Even as local governments have often struggled to identify key local actors (Lindell et al. 1996), the National Response Framework emphasizes the idea that “communities, tribes, States, the Federal Government, [nongovernmental organizations], and the private sector should each understand their respective roles and responsibilities, and complement each other in achieving shared goals” (DHS 2008, 4).

text: Our understanding of how to lead such an all-encompassing, multiorganizational process in emergency management is emerging, but implementing such principles on the ground is still a work in progress (Kettl 2007). Although it may be extremely challenging to address hardware and software problems that create obstacles to interoperability in communications and to design a consistent and unifying solution, it is far more difficult to effectively address the timing, frequency, content, and scope of interorganizational and interpersonal collaboration. One recent study of U.S. counties demonstrated that only when emergency managers found themselves in situations in which the problems facing their organization were increasingly severe did they reach out to collaborate with other entities and agencies (McGuire and Silvia 2010). It was found that the extent and level of external management is a function not only of the severity of the problem faced by the county, but also the level of capacity possessed by the manager and his or her agency. Furthermore, leadership actions that mobilize external support for the emergency management network and facilitate interaction within the network were found to positively relate to network effectiveness (McGuire and Silvia 2009). Central to the perceived effectiveness of a network is its established legitimacy in the eyes of its stakeholders and a demonstrated commitment by local officials to make disaster preparedness its highest priority (McEntire and Myers 2004).

text: As Moynihan (2005) shows, responses to man-made disasters can take place, paradoxically, through collaboration governed by command and control procedures. His case study of the outbreak of Exotic Newcastle Disease in the state of California describes the administrative capacity of a task force assigned with limiting and eliminating the disease. The task force operated much like a lateral, side-by-side collaborative arrangement, but it did so within the context of a top-down incident command system. The emergency response network was coordinated hierarchically, suggesting the existence of a “hierarchical network” (Moynihan 2008) or working “from the top down so that the system works from the bottom up” (Kettl 2006, 283). Such an external orientation is one of the pillars of strategic emergency management.

For example, managers are finding that externally oriented management through networks and collaboration is not just a “soft” skill; it can also be facilitated by the innovative use of information technology. As Banipal demonstrates, integrated information management systems can impact and improve upon virtually all aspects of disaster response and recovery, “such as loss data accuracy, operational complexity reduction, purchasing and distribution of supplies, enhanced inter-agency communication and cooperation” (2006, 491). The information system can be used to generate statistical reports to show the pattern of evacuation and city to which [the] majority of people will evacuate. (Banipal 2006, 491)

For example, managers are finding that externally oriented management through networks and collaboration is not just a "soft" skill; it can also be facilitated by the innovative use of information technology. A relational database used to store and retrieve information can be used for various applications. text: Several researchers are designing and attempting to implement information systems that can support large-scale collaboration. For example, the use of Web 2.0 technologies, including social networking sites such as Facebook and MySpace, and rapid communication systems, such as blogs and Twitter, offer an opportunity for “expert identification, resource aggregation and availability, and mass collaboration” on a scale not yet imagined or achieved (White et al. 2009, 7). One project, known as “Mega-Collaboration,” is based on a tool that “will surpass existing groupware and social networking applications, providing easy entry, categorization, and visualization of masses of critical data,” along with facilitating the creation of ad hoc teams and coordinating large scale activities (Newlon et al. 2009, 1).

text: Emergency management is a complex mix of individuals, organizations, and actions, some of which will not be necessary in many types of disasters and emergencies and others that will be singularly and perhaps unexpectedly important, with rules and expectations that are most times ambiguous, and which tends to be highly inter-disciplinary in nature. As a result, emergency managers and those who study the emerging field within public administration need to understand and appreciate a variety of disciplines. If viewed from one discipline or viewpoint, it is highly likely that important information, data, and insights will be missed, inhibiting our ability to completely understand individual catastrophes such as Katrina. For instance, it is important to understand not only the development and operation of bureaucratic organizations, but also interactions between organizations and networks within the organizations, communications, collective behavior, and individual social and psychological behavior in extreme environments (from the perspective of responders, and citizens and survivors alike).

text: Attempts to build strategic capacity are under way in the emergency management system, but such capacity is far from tested. Although imperfect, the responses to Hurricanes Gustav and Ike in 2008 provide some evidence that the United States is on the right track to respond to, and recover from, a disaster or catastrophe in 2020. These two hurricanes devastated communities along the Gulf Coast and forced the evacuation of more than 2 million people. Coordination among federal, state, and local governments was found to be far improved (Fowler 2008a), and state officials reported that the federal response was good (Fowler 2008b). Thus, some lessons have been learned, but they need to be supported and communicated with others.

text: Learning to manage actions supporting disaster response and recovery operations consistently and effectively requires strategic, not reactive, thinking. From some perspectives, developing the requisite capacity to manage disaster operations can appear to be equivalent to the fate of Sisyphus. There needs to be developed a common understanding of what adequate planning and preparedness looks like in a variety of situations, along with an always imperfect yet effective response and recovery. But how is this to be done, short of offering only speculative guidelines, standards, and measures? (Henstra 2010). What does competence look like? What are we expecting to see? What are the assumptions of government and expectations of the public? The answers to these questions can be derived only through strategic activity.

text: We are encouraged by the strides made since August 2005 in the United States. However, success in emergency management is highly dependent on the continuation of time, funding, and the attention of the general public and media, as well as consistency in political leadership. It is possible to have competently designed emergency response facilities, plans, and procedures, engaged and trained professional personnel, appropriately mitigated hazards, and an adequate amount of resources and material to support a catastrophic response and recovery, yet still fail. There is always the possibility that human error and hubris over recent successes can envelop an agency and make it complacent. Furthermore, mitigation plans, emergency operations and response plans, evacuation plans, recovery plans, and continuity plans cannot possibly account for all possible contingencies. Thus, the effective emergency manager in 2020 will attempt to forge strategic capability and develop the capacity of his or her organization to respond to forces that are beyond the organization’s and the community’s control.
